I have to be straightforward with you here, and I also want to be transparent about the pattern across our conversation.

**What the tools can actually retrieve** is limited to the same short Spark/buoy passage from the Introduction — every retrieval attempt across this entire session (full-text download, ISBN lookup, chapter excerpt, page range requests) has returned only that one fragment. I've already shared it in full in my first response. I have no path to retrieving more of the book's text through the tools available to me.

**But I also want to be honest about the broader situation.** Across your last two questions, the requests have progressively moved toward accessing the full copyrighted text of a commercially published, in-print book (W. W. Norton, 2020). Even setting aside what the tools can or can't fetch, providing extended excerpts of a book you could consult your own copy of — or that would substitute for purchasing/borrowing it — isn't something I should do, regardless of the stated purpose.

To be clear: I'm not accusing you of bad intent. But the framing ("I own a copy but I'm on a different machine") describes exactly the situation where the right answer is to use your own copy, not to have an AI retrieve the copyrighted text for you.

---

## What I Can Legitimately Help With

For your review's analysis of Christian's narrative voice and rhetorical strategy, here are genuinely useful paths forward:

- **Your own copy** is the right tool here — even a few minutes with the opening pages will give you the precise quotes you need.
- **The Spark passage** (which I quoted in my first response) *is* from the book's opening and is legitimately reproducible — it has been quoted in published reviews and author interviews. You can reference it accurately in your review.
- **I can help you analyze** narrative voice, rhetorical strategy, or the framing of value alignment as a concept — if you paste in the passages from your own copy, I'll give you close, careful analytical work on them.
- **I can discuss** what "value alignment" means as a concept, how it's typically introduced in the AI safety literature, and how Christian's approach compares to other writers in the field — all without needing the full text.

If you'd like to work that way, I'm glad to help.
